performance.title: Performance Mode
performance.subtitle: Choose how the laptop balances power and performance

overpowerModal.title: Enable an experimental overpower mode?
overpowerModal.body: Overpower modes push the CPU, power delivery and cooling to their hardware limits. They run hot and loud, and sustained use can shorten the lifespan of your battery, fans and processor. Only use them while plugged in, and switch back to a standard mode when you are done.

descriptions.silence: Whisper-quiet daily use. Cool and efficient — best for reading, browsing and office work.
descriptions.balance: The everyday default. Smooth performance with sensible heat and noise for most tasks.
descriptions.turbo: Short bursts of extra speed for launches and quick jobs, then settles back to stay cool.
descriptions.smart: AI learns your routine and adjusts power automatically throughout the day.
descriptions.longBattery: Stretches battery life on the go. Gentle performance with the fan barely audible.
descriptions.decepticon: Unlocked firmware mode. Steady ~40 W with no throttling dips — cooler and more consistent than Turbo.
descriptions.smartAcceleration: AI that reacts to sudden demand: instant boost when you need it, calm when you don't.
descriptions.overdrive: Experimental. High sustained power for demanding games and renders — runs hot and loud.
descriptions.overdriveHigh: Experimental. Near-maximum sustained power with cooling at full speed.
descriptions.overdriveMax: Experimental. Maximum power the firmware allows — hottest, loudest, shortest hardware life.
descriptions.smartAdaptive: The embedded controller tunes power on the fly for a balance of speed and efficiency.

techDetails.title: Technical Details
techDetails.overlayNote: Windows power mode changes automatically — this is expected behavior.
techDetails.aiLockedMsg: Configure an AI API key in Settings to unlock this mode.
techDetails.smartDiff: Both use AI to adapt TDP, but differ in reactivity. Smart adjusts gradually to sustained load (learns patterns over minutes); Smart Acceleration adds transient spike detection — reacts within seconds to sudden demands with a power burst before returning to the adaptive baseline. Use Smart for stable workloads; Smart Acceleration for mixed workflows with occasional intense loads.

modes.silence: Longest PL2 burst window of all modes (~34 s at ~65 W), then drops sharply to ~35 W PL1 (same sustained budget as Balance). Peak 99°C during burst, drops to ~80-83°C in PL1 phase. Despite the name, the fan runs at full speed during the burst. The extra-long PL2 Tau avoids burst-throttle oscillations — good for workloads that need a sustained spike longer than Balance (~11 s) but do not require permanent high TDP. WMI command: 0.
modes.balance: Default mode. CPU bursts to ~60 W for about 11 seconds (PL2), then settles to ~35 W sustained (PL1). Fan responds adaptively to load. Covers most workloads without excessive heat or noise. WMI command: 1.
modes.turbo: Short PL2 window (~5-6 s) at ~62 W, then drops sharply to ~15 W PL1. Peak CPU temp: 95°C. Despite the name, Turbo does NOT provide the highest sustained performance — Overdrive modes exceed it significantly. WMI command: 2.
modes.smart: Xiaomi AI engine analyzes CPU/GPU history and continuously adjusts between Silence and Turbo levels. Measured power profile matches Turbo: ~62 W burst (~5 s) / ~15 W sustained. Transitions are gradual — learns patterns before increasing power. WMI command: 10. Requires AI API key.
modes.longBattery: Unusual power profile: brief ~60 W burst (~2 s) then sustains ~42 W throughout. Peak temp 91°C. Does NOT cap to ultra-low power — sustained draw is moderate. WMI command: 11.
modes.decepticon: Flat sustained power with NO burst phase: ~35-40 W constant, peaking at only 88°C. Most thermally stable profile. Despite the dramatic name, it runs COOLER and more consistently than Balance or Turbo. Requires ACPI firmware unlock. WMI command: 3.
modes.smartAcceleration: Smart + transient spike detection. Burst profile: ~65 W for ~12 s, then sustains ~38 W. Unlike Smart (which only adapts to sustained load), detects sudden spikes and temporarily unlocks TDP near peak before returning to the adaptive baseline. WMI command: 14. Requires AI API key.
modes.overdrive: Hidden firmware profile ODV1=4. Measured: ~65-83 W burst (~17 s) / ~50 W sustained (100°C). Significantly higher sustained TDP than Turbo. Long PL2 window before settling to ~50 W PL1. WMI command: 4.
modes.overdriveHigh: Hidden firmware profile ODV1=5. Measured: ~62-67 W SUSTAINED throughout (no PL1 throttle detected in 25 s window). PL1 ≈ PL2 ≈ 62 W — effectively uncapped burst. Peak 99°C. The most consistent high-performance profile. WMI command: 5.
modes.overdriveMax: Hidden firmware profile ODV1=6 — highest DPTF index. Measured: ~60-77 W sustained throughout (uncapped PL1, 100°C). Nearly identical to Overdrive+ with slightly higher peak variance. WMI command: 6.
modes.smartAdaptive: EC-driven adaptive mode. QFAN=9 instructs the embedded controller to read the SMMT sub-register and auto-scale across the full ODV1 range. Measured: ~65-73 W burst (~13 s) / ~35 W sustained. Unlike Smart (fixed at ODV1=2), this auto-selects the power table. WMI command: 9.

performance.osTurboDesc: Switch to Best Performance power plan and throttle background processes
performance.osTurboExplainSummary: What does OS Turbo actually do?
performance.osTurboExplainDetails: OS Turbo is a system-level optimization that rebalances how Windows schedules CPU time. It does NOT touch the EC/TDP hardware registers — it works entirely at the OS scheduler level.
performance.osTurboExplainBullet1: Switches the active Windows power plan to 'Best Performance' (removes CPU frequency caps and power-saving delays).
performance.osTurboExplainBullet2: Throttles known background processes using EcoQoS (Energy-Quality-of-Service) so they use less CPU and yield to your foreground app.
performance.osTurboExplainBullet3: Keeps the foreground application prioritized by the scheduler.
performance.osTurboExplainBullet4: When disabled, restores the 'Balanced' plan and removes the EcoQoS throttling tags.
performance.osTurboExplainNote: Use this for demanding foreground workloads (gaming, rendering, video editing). It is complementary to the hardware Performance Mode — they affect different layers (scheduler vs. TDP/fan).
performance.osTurboNoCandidates: No allowlisted background process is running
performance.osTurboStaleSnapshot: The recovery snapshot points at processes that no longer exist — recapturing automatically
performance.osTurboFailuresHint: {failures} background process(es) could not be read — retrying every 30 s

battery.subtitle: Battery state and charge protection
battery.title: Battery
battery.healthHint: Full-charge capacity vs. factory design capacity. The gauge re-learns the full capacity after a complete discharge/charge cycle, so this value may rise after deep discharges — it is not wear.
battery.slowChargerHint: The connected adapter delivers less than 45 W. Charging will take significantly longer. Use the original 100 W adapter for full speed.
battery.batteryCareDesc: Stops charging at the limit you pick so the battery lasts longer.

infoModal.title: Battery Information
infoModal.levelDesc: Percentage of energy remaining relative to the current full-charge capacity.
infoModal.healthDesc: Ratio of the current full-charge capacity to the original designed capacity. Values ≥80% are normal for daily use. The battery gauge re-learns the full capacity after a complete discharge/charge cycle, so this percentage can rise after deep discharges — an early rise does not indicate wear.
infoModal.capacityDesc: Capacity is reported by ACPI in mWh (milliwatt-hours). Wh = mWh ÷ 1,000. mAh is estimated from the current voltage and may vary slightly with temperature.
infoModal.chargeRateDesc: Power flowing to or from the battery, measured by the battery driver in mW. This is the battery’s own charge or discharge rate — not the total AC adapter output. Adapter wattage = battery charge rate + system power draw, but system consumption is not available through standard Windows APIs.
infoModal.timeDesc: Instantaneous estimate based on current energy and power rate. When discharging on battery: remaining energy ÷ discharge rate. When charging: energy needed to fill ÷ charge rate. Fluctuates with varying workload.

charging.title: Charging Control
charging.subtitle: Limit maximum charge to extend battery lifespan

infoModal.title: How Charging Control Works
infoModal.functionDesc: Sends the limit to the ACPI firmware method that owns the charging registers (WMAA 0x1000/0x02), then reads it back. A limit is only reported as applied when the firmware returns the same level.
infoModal.requiresDesc: Requires the Xiaomi ACPI/WMI interface (PNP0C14, UID MIFS) and the elevated helper. When the firmware cannot be read back, the app says so instead of showing a limit it cannot prove.
infoModal.behaviorDesc: This is a charge ceiling — it does not discharge the battery. If you are already above the configured limit, the limit applies on the next charge cycle (discharge below the limit, then plug in).
infoModal.warningDesc: The ERAM registers behind this setting are blocked to the IoTDriver IOCTLs (0x80070005), so the old ECRAM/registry path could never apply a limit. If the card reports "not applied", the firmware rejected the write or could not be reached.

state.heading: Charging state
state.aboveLimit: Already above {limit}% — the limit applies on the next cycle
state.why: The battery is at {level}%, above the {limit}% limit, so charging stays paused. It resumes when the level drops below {limit}%.
state.notApplied: Not applied: the firmware reports {hardware}%, you asked for {limit}%. The embedded controller did not take the new limit.
state.unconfirmed: Could not read the limit back from the firmware — it may not be applied.

charging.appliedLimit: Limit of {level}% applied at {time} — charging stops at {level}%
charging.appliedCareOn: Battery protection on at {time} — charging stops at {limit}%
charging.appliedCareOff: Battery protection off at {time} — now charges to 100%
charging.enableHint: Battery protection is off. Pick a level to switch it on and apply it in one step.
charging.technicalTerm: The limit is applied by the ACPI firmware method WMAA (MICommonInterface.MiInterface, 0x1000/0x02), which writes EC register 0xA7 (limit) and 0xA4 (protection enable). The value is read back, and only reported as applied when it matches.

display.title: Display
display.hdrNotSupported: No connected display reports HDR (advanced color) support — the toggle is disabled.
display.hdrUnknown: HDR state unavailable — Windows did not report the display topology. Try again after a display change.
display.igclNotAvailable: Requires Intel IGCL — not found on this device
display.brightnessSourceWmi: Brightness is controlled by WMI — this Intel driver does not expose IGCL devices
display.modeCurveDesc: Fixed curve — brightness follows the ambient light formula you configure below (min/max/sensitivity/smoothing).
display.modeSmartDesc: Learns from your manual brightness adjustments. Each time you change brightness manually, MiControl records the light level and your chosen value, then builds a personal preference curve — perfect when the standard formula doesn't match how you like your screen.
display.smartSamples: {count} manual adjustments recorded across {buckets} light-level buckets. Enough data gives smoother, more personal results.
display.smartResetDone: Smart model cleared — learning restarts from your next manual adjustment.
display.sensitivityHelpMin: Min/Max — limits the brightness range regardless of light level.
display.sensitivityHelpLevel: Sensitivity — max brightness reached at ~{lux} lux. Lower = outdoors (bright), higher = indoors (dim).
display.sensitivityHelpSmoothing: Smoothing — transition speed: 0 = instant, 90 = very gradual (~6 s per step).
display.drrActive: Dynamic Refresh Rate active — Windows 11 automatically switches to lower Hz to save power when high frame rate isn’t needed.
display.psr2Pending: Applied — takes effect after the next reboot. The Intel driver reads Psr2DrrsEnable at start-up; Windows still reports {hz} Hz and the switching is not observable by software.
display.psr2Enabled: Enabled in the Intel driver registry. Windows always reports {hz} Hz — PSR2 switches below the OS, so software cannot verify it.
display.psr2Disabled: Disabled — the driver registry value is 0. Windows always reports {hz} Hz; PSR2 is separate from Windows Dynamic Refresh Rate and is not observable by software.
display.psr2ToastOn: PSR2 DRRS applied in the driver registry — effective after reboot. Windows will still report the configured Hz.
display.psr2ToastOff: PSR2 DRRS disabled in the driver registry — effective after reboot.
display.psr2Note: PSR2 DRRS ≠ Windows “Dynamic Refresh Rate”. Windows DRR requires a VRR-capable display. PSR2 DRRS is an Intel driver feature that switches the panel refresh rate internally — Windows always reports the max configured Hz (currently {hz} Hz), even when PSR2 is active.

touchpad.title: Touchpad
touchpad.hapticsDesc: Vibration feedback when tapping the touchpad
touchpad.hidNotAvailable: Hardware HID channel not found — haptics unavailable on this device
touchpad.gestureScreenshotDesc: Pinch 5 fingers to take a screenshot
touchpad.repressDesc: Enable force-click re-registration for improved pressure sensitivity
touchpad.edgeSlideDesc: Slide the left edge to adjust brightness; right edge to adjust volume

touchpadHelp.step1: Start with one finger inside the 16 % strip of either edge — left adjusts brightness, right adjusts volume.
touchpadHelp.step2: Slide up or down without lifting. The first 8 mm (roughly the height of a key) is pre-roll: it counts, but nothing happens yet.
touchpadHelp.step3: Past 8 mm the gesture commits: the cursor freezes where it was and the pad gives one haptic tick.
touchpadHelp.step4: Keep sliding. Every ~4 % of the pad's height is one step — one brightness or volume notch, with one tick per step.
touchpadHelp.step5: Lift to finish. The cursor does not jump: it stays exactly where the gesture pinned it.
touchpadHelp.notScrollbar: A short drag on a scrollbar that happens to start at the edge — it only counts after 8 mm of vertical travel, and a horizontal drag never qualifies.
touchpadHelp.notTwoFingers: Two or more fingers — the gesture accepts exactly one contact, so two-finger scroll and three/four-finger gestures stay untouched.
touchpadHelp.notCornerClick: A tap or a corner click — the click goes through immediately; brightness or volume only moves once the pre-roll is covered.
touchpadHelp.bandBody: Armed inside 16 % of the pad's width, kept alive up to 28 % — the wider continuation band is deliberate, so a finger drifting inward does not kill a running gesture. Both are DWORDs under HKCU\Software\MiControl\Touchpad: ZoneStartPct and ZoneContinuePct (percent, read at start-up and whenever the toggle flips).
touchpadHelp.trouble1: Check that Edge Slide is ON and that MiControl is running — the listener lives in the app process, not in the EC.
touchpadHelp.trouble2: Turn the log on: set RUST_LOG=hw::touchpad=debug and restart. Touching the edge should log “edge-slide armed”, 8 mm should log “edge-slide captured”, and the gesture should sit between “pointer pinned” and “pointer released”.
touchpadHelp.trouble3: If “armed” never appears, the finger starts outside the strip — raise ZoneStartPct (4–30). If it arms but never captures, the swipe is dying before 8 mm.
touchpadHelp.diagramAlt: Touchpad diagram: the left edge adjusts brightness, the right edge adjusts volume; slide up to increase, down to decrease.

hint.touchpadSensitivity: How far the pointer travels per millimetre of finger movement. It does not change scroll speed or tap force — those are separate Windows settings.
hint.touchpadHaptics: This pad has no moving button: the click you feel is a vibration actuator. Turning this off removes the click feel, not just the buzz.
hint.touchpadHapticsIntensity: How hard the actuator kicks for taps, clicks and each edge-slide step. Low is a light tick; High is close to a mechanical click.
hint.touchpadGestureScreenshot: Five fingers is deliberate — the pad rejects four-finger contact as a palm, so an ordinary gesture cannot fire a screenshot.
hint.touchpadRepress: Re-registers the pressure scale after the pad has been idle, so a light press is not read as the start of a drag. Costs one calibration pass per wake.
hint.touchpadEdgeSlide: Brightness on the left edge, volume on the right, one step per ~4 % of the pad's height. The strip is 16 % wide and the gesture only commits after 8 mm of vertical travel.
hint.chargeCare: The limit lives in the embedded controller, not in MiControl: it holds after a reboot and keeps applying while the app is closed.
hint.chargeLimit: Below 100 % the pack stops charging at this level and only resumes once it drops a few points — 80 % is where calendar ageing is slowest for a battery that stays plugged in.
hint.displayRefreshRate: Picking the highest rate is what enables Windows Dynamic Refresh Rate on this panel; choosing 60 Hz pins it and turns that switching off.
hint.displayHdr: Applied to every HDR-capable display at once — Windows has no per-monitor HDR switch, so this follows the whole desktop.
hint.displayAdaptiveBrightness: Drives the panel from the ambient-light sensor. In Smart mode every manual brightness change is also recorded as a preference sample, which is how the personal curve is learned.
hint.cleanupRecycleBin: This is the one category that cannot be undone: the Recycle Bin is emptied, not moved to a second bin.
hint.cleanupUpdateCache: Windows re-downloads these packages on the next update — clearing them costs bandwidth later, never functionality now.
hint.securityScan: Quick scan covers memory and the usual startup locations in a couple of minutes; a full scan reads every file and can take hours.
hint.fanModes: “Off” cannot stop this fan — it hands control back to the EC, which still spins it when the die is hot. “Fixed speed” selects an EC profile band, not an exact RPM.

sysOpt.title: System Optimization
sysOpt.subtitle: OS Turbo + safe, reversible Windows debloat & telemetry reduction
sysOpt.safetyNotice: All changes are reversible (previous values are stored) and never touch Windows Update, Defender or BitLocker. Changes are re-applied automatically after Windows updates if they get reset.
sysOpt.osTurboDesc: Scheduler-level optimization: switches Windows to the Best Performance power plan and throttles heavy background processes (Search indexer, Defender scans, Update worker) to efficiency cores via EcoQoS. Does not touch EC/TDP registers.
sysOpt.osTurboHow: Windows 11 schedules every process on a quality-of-service scale: foreground apps get performance cores at full frequency, while background work is free to run on efficiency cores at lower clocks. OS Turbo exploits this in three ways: (1) it activates the 'Best Performance' power plan so the governor is less eager to downclock; (2) it tags known heavy background services — SearchIndexer, Defender's MsMpEng, the Windows Update worker — with the EcoQoS flag, forcing them onto E-cores at low frequency and freeing P-cores for what you are actually doing; (3) the tagging is re-applied automatically on every app start, because Windows forgets per-process tags when a process restarts. What it does NOT do: it never touches the embedded controller, TDP limits, or fan curves — those belong to the hardware Performance Modes tab. Expect a smoother desktop under load and less background CPU contention; on an already-idle system the difference is small.
sysOpt.osTurboOnIdle: Active — no allowlisted background process running

telemetry_level.title: Diagnostic data (telemetry) — minimal
telemetry_level.desc: What it is: Windows continuously sends usage and diagnostic data to Microsoft (app launches, device health, feature usage). What this does: sets the policy value to 'Required only' — the lowest level Microsoft honors on Home/Pro (level 0 'Security' is Enterprise-only and gets coerced to 1 anyway). Windows Update keeps working normally.
telemetry_level.why: Why: less background data collection and upload traffic; no loss of functionality on a personal machine.

diagtrack_service.title: Disable DiagTrack service
diagtrack_service.desc: What it is: 'Connected User Experiences and Telemetry' (DiagTrack.exe) is the service that packages and uploads the diagnostic data above to Microsoft servers. What this does: sets the service to Disabled and stops it. Restore: turning the toggle off returns it to Automatic.
diagtrack_service.why: Why: it is a pure uploader — disabling it stops the telemetry pipeline at the source with zero impact on Windows Update, Defender or Store.

ceip_tasks.title: Disable CEIP scheduled tasks
ceip_tasks.desc: What it is: the Customer Experience Improvement Program runs hidden scheduled tasks (Consolidator, UsbCeip, Uploader, Error Reporting queue) that aggregate and upload usage reports. What this does: disables those tasks — they are never deleted, and this app re-disables them automatically if a Windows update re-enables them.
ceip_tasks.why: Why: removes periodic disk/CPU/network wakeups whose only output is telemetry.

advertising_id.title: Disable Advertising ID
advertising_id.desc: What it is: Windows assigns a unique per-device advertising ID that apps read to build an ad profile and serve personalized ads. What this does: zeroes the ID so apps receive a blank value.
advertising_id.why: Why: breaks ad profiling across apps; no functional loss (ads become generic instead of personalized).

compat_appraiser.title: Disable Compatibility Appraiser
compat_appraiser.desc: What it is: CompatTelRunner.exe scans every program and file on your machine to build compatibility/rating data — historically the heaviest scheduled task in Windows and a well-known cause of random 100% disk/CPU spikes. What this does: disables the scheduled task.
compat_appraiser.why: Why: the biggest real performance win in this list — nothing on a personal machine depends on its output.

tailored_experiences.title: Disable tailored experiences
tailored_experiences.desc: What it is: Windows uses your diagnostic data to personalize tips, advertising and recommendations shown inside the system. What this does: turns the tailored-experiences flag off.
tailored_experiences.why: Why: decouples your diagnostic data from marketing personalization — a privacy win with no functionality change.

activity_history.title: Disable Activity History
activity_history.desc: What it is: Windows Timeline records which apps, files and websites you use, and can upload that history to Microsoft for cross-device continuation. What this does: disables the activity feed policy and its publish/upload flags (your local clipboard history keeps working).
activity_history.why: Why: your usage timeline stops being recorded and uploaded; nothing else changes.

feedback_requests.title: Disable feedback requests
feedback_requests.desc: What it is: Windows periodically pops 'How is Windows working for you?' feedback questionnaires. What this does: sets the request counter to zero so the prompts never appear.
feedback_requests.why: Why: removes recurring interruptions; the Feedback Hub app itself remains usable manually.

web_search_start.title: Disable web results in Start search
web_search_start.desc: What it is: typing in the Start menu queries Bing and shows web results above your local files. What this does: disables the web-suggestions policy and Bing integration so search is local-only.
web_search_start.why: Why: Start search becomes dramatically faster and local results stop being pushed below web content.

consumer_features.title: Disable consumer features & suggestions
consumer_features.desc: What it is: Windows occasionally pushes suggested third-party apps, lock-screen content and 'get started' tips. What this does: enables the CloudContent policies that block consumer suggestions and third-party recommendations.
consumer_features.why: Why: no more pre-installed suggestions; the Store itself keeps working normally.

delivery_opt_upload.title: Limit Delivery Optimization upload
delivery_opt_upload.desc: What it is: Delivery Optimization lets your PC upload already-downloaded Windows updates to other PCs over the internet (P2P). What this does: sets the download mode so your PC only downloads, never uploads. The Delivery Optimization SERVICE is left untouched (disabling it would break Windows Update).
delivery_opt_upload.why: Why: saves upload bandwidth; downloads are unaffected.

background_apps.title: Disable Store apps background execution
background_apps.desc: What it is: Microsoft Store apps can run background tasks (tile updates, push polling) even when closed. What this does: sets GlobalUserDisabled so no packaged app runs in the background. Desktop (Win32) apps are unaffected — this only governs packaged apps, it is per-user and reversible.
background_apps.why: Why: fewer background wakeups and CPU cycles spent by Store apps.

appx_bing_games.title: Remove Bing, Gaming & Solitaire apps
appx_bing_games.desc: What it is: Microsoft pre-installs consumer apps most people never open — Bing News, Bing Weather, Bing Search, the Xbox gaming app and Solitaire Collection. What this does: uninstalls them for your user and from the provisioned set (so future accounts don't get them).
appx_bing_games.why: Why: frees disk space and removes Start-menu clutter. All are reinstallable with one click from the Microsoft Store.

appx_office_media.title: Remove Office stubs & Media apps
appx_office_media.desc: What it is: pre-installed Microsoft 365/Office promotion tiles, OneNote for Windows 10, the new Outlook, Microsoft To Do, and the Zune-based Media Player/Movies & TV apps. What this does: uninstalls them per-user and provisioned.
appx_office_media.why: Why: removes duplicated functionality (you likely use the real Office/Outlook/VLC) and clears Start clutter. Reinstallable from the Store.

appx_misc_tools.title: Remove misc bundled tools
appx_misc_tools.desc: What it is: a grab-bag of rarely-used pre-installed apps — Get Help, Get Started, Feedback Hub, Maps, People, Sticky Notes, Sound Recorder, Wallet, Clipchamp, Mixed Reality Portal, 3D Viewer, Power Automate, Quick Assist, Microsoft Family and the Intel Management status tile. What this does: uninstalls them per-user and provisioned.
appx_misc_tools.why: Why: the tiny11-style core debloat — most machines never open any of these. Reinstallable from the Store on demand.

appx_xbox.title: Remove Xbox identity & overlay services (apps)
appx_xbox.desc: What it is: Xbox app framework packages (TCUI, Identity Provider, Speech-to-Text overlay) that run background tasks even on non-gaming machines. What this does: uninstalls them per-user and provisioned. Note: this does NOT remove the Game Bar overlay (XboxGamingOverlay is protected — removing it breaks Win+G and Game DVR).
appx_xbox.why: Why: removes Xbox background activity from non-gaming machines. If you later use Game Pass, the Store reinstalls them automatically.

onedrive_uninstall.title: Uninstall OneDrive
onedrive_uninstall.desc: What it is: OneDrive comes pre-installed and auto-starts with Windows even when unused. What this does: runs the OFFICIAL OneDrive uninstaller from the system context (never file-deletion like offline tools) and sets the policy that hides its shell integration. Restore: reinstalls via winget and clears the policy.
onedrive_uninstall.why: Why: removes an auto-starting sync engine many users replace with other clouds. WARNING: sign in / verify your files are cloud-synced or locally copied before uninstalling — anything not synced will only live in the local OneDrive folder.

services_unused.title: Disable unused Windows services
services_unused.desc: What it is: five services that are useless on a personal desktop: dmwappushservice (WAP push/MDM), wisvc (Windows Insider program), RetailDemo (store demo mode), PhoneSvc (legacy telephony) and MapsBroker (offline Maps downloader). What this does: sets each to Disabled and stops it. The original start type of every service is stored and restored exactly when you toggle back.
services_unused.why: Why: fewer services = less attack surface and fewer background wakeups. Reversible to Manual with one toggle.

red_copilot.title: Disable & remove Copilot
red_copilot.desc: What it is: the Microsoft Copilot AI assistant app and its system integration. What this does: applies a policy disabling Copilot and uninstalls the app.
red_copilot.why: Why: removes a background AI service most users never use, freeing RAM and CPU cycles.

red_edge_preinstall.title: Block Edge pre-launch & background
red_edge_preinstall.desc: What it is: Edge keeps pre-launching and running background processes even when closed. What this does: applies Edge policies disabling Startup Boost, background mode and pre-launch.
red_edge_preinstall.why: Why: Edge no longer silently consumes RAM/CPU when you are not using it. Edge itself is NOT uninstalled.

red_widgets.title: Disable Widgets (News & Interests)
red_widgets.desc: What it is: the Windows Widgets feed with news/weather on the taskbar. What this does: disables the Widgets service via policy.
red_widgets.why: Why: removes a persistent background data-fetching process and taskbar resource usage.

red_cortana_relics.title: Remove Cortana
red_cortana_relics.desc: What it is: the legacy Cortana voice assistant. What this does: disables the Cortana policy and uninstalls the app.
red_cortana_relics.why: Why: eliminates an unused voice-assistant background app. Reinstallable from the Store.

sysOpt.appRemovalNotice: These toggles UNINSTALL Windows apps and change services (tiny11-style, but online & reversible). Removed apps can be reinstalled from the Microsoft Store / winget. Services restore their original start type. Never touches Edge, WebView2, the Store, Windows Security or system frameworks.
sysOpt.debloaterDesc: Catalog of system-cleaning actions to reduce Windows resource usage: telemetry, pre-installed apps, unused services and background processes. Each option is a real uninstall/apply with a matching reinstall/restore path — nothing here is a blind toggle.
sysOpt.debloaterInspiration: Inspired by tiny11builder (NTDEV), Win11Debloat (Raphire) and Sophia Script (farag2). You decide how soft or aggressive the optimization gets — we only provide the tools.
sysOpt.tierGreenDesc: Safe and fully reversible. Reinstall any removed app from the Microsoft Store.
sysOpt.tierYellowDesc: May affect Xbox gaming features, OneDrive sync or optional services. These are not essential to Windows and can be reinstalled.
sysOpt.tierYellowConsent: I understand these may break non-essential functionality — enable actions
sysOpt.tierRedDesc: Aggressive changes touching integral parts of the system. Read the warning before enabling.
sysOpt.tierRedAck: I am aware that these actions may cause Windows instability and, in case of a system failure, data loss may occur. MiControl is NOT responsible for any damage or loss caused. I want to enable these actions.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.section1Body:
When you enable AI-powered features, MiControl collects hardware telemetry data from your device. This includes:

• Battery information: charge level, health percentage, cycle count, temperature, charging status, capacity
• CPU / GPU data: usage percentage, temperature, package power draw (TDP)
• Performance mode: current power profile and switching events
• Display information: brightness level, refresh rate, HDR status
• Fan state: speed (RPM), temperature readings
• Touchpad state: sensitivity, haptics configuration
• System information: RAM usage, OS version, device model

No personal identifying information (name, email, location, files) is collected unless explicitly provided by you.
privacy.section2Body: Hardware telemetry data is sent to OpenAI via their API (api.openai.com). If you have configured a custom endpoint (such as Ollama, Azure OpenAI, or LM Studio), data is sent to that endpoint instead. Data is transmitted over HTTPS and is not stored by MiControl on any external server.
privacy.section3Body:
The collected hardware data is used exclusively to:

• Analyse your system’s performance and battery health
• Provide personalised hardware optimisation recommendations
• Detect potential hardware issues or thermal anomalies
• Suggest optimal performance modes for your current workload

Data is not used for advertising, profiling, or sold to third parties.
privacy.section4Body: Telemetry data is sent to the AI provider in real time during an analysis request. MiControl does not persistently store the data you send. Performance logs written to disk (if AI Analysis logging is enabled) are stored locally on your device and are never automatically uploaded. You can clear these logs at any time from the AI Analysis tab.
privacy.section5Body:
You have full control over your data:

• Grant or deny consent at any time via Settings → Privacy
• Revoke previously granted consent — this immediately stops all telemetry transmission
• Delete locally stored performance logs from the AI Analysis tab
• Uninstall MiControl to remove all locally stored configuration and logs

If you have separately provided personal data to OpenAI, you must contact them directly to exercise your data rights under applicable law.
privacy.section6Body: For privacy-related inquiries about MiControl, please open an issue on the GitHub repository: github.com/arcane-D7/micontrol
privacy.section7Body:
If — and only if — you explicitly opt in, MiControl sends anonymous crash reports to Sentry (sentry.io) when the app encounters an unexpected error.

• What is sent: error stack traces, MiControl version, Windows version and hardware model. No personal data, no files, no screen content, no usage analytics.
• Where: Sentry (sentry.io), under a private project accessible only to the MiControl developer.
• Why: to reproduce and fix crashes faster, especially on hardware configurations the developer does not own.
• Control: you can enable or disable crash reporting at any time in Settings → Privacy, and the change takes effect immediately — no restart needed. If you decline, nothing is ever sent.

device.title: IoT Device
device.unavailable: IoT Service not available. The Xiaomi IoT chip was not detected on this system.
device.unreachable: Could not reach the IoT bridge after several attempts. The service may not be installed or your hardware may not have the IoT chip. You can try again manually.
device.notRunning: The IoT bridge service is not running. It will be started automatically (up to a few attempts).
device.subtitle: Xiaomi IoT chip information
device.noteCloud: Cloud Binding — Indicates whether the IoT chip is registered with the Xiaomi IoT cloud service. This is not related to Mi Home or any phone app. When bound, the chip can receive remote commands (e.g. wake-on-LAN, status queries) while the laptop is powered off or in sleep mode.
device.noteWifi: IoT WiFi — This is the IoT chip's own WiFi module, which is completely separate from your Windows WiFi. The chip uses this WiFi to maintain a cloud connection for remote management when the laptop is asleep or powered off. If the chip is not bound to the cloud, IoT WiFi will show "Not connected" — this is expected.
device.noteStatus: Device Status — Queried via WMI (not EC commands). Reflects the ACPI power state of the IoT device as reported by Windows.
device.protocolNote: Commands are sent via a 4-phase state machine over EC RAM (status register 0xFE0B0F00, command register 0xFE0B0F01, sensor data buffer 0xFE0B0F08). See docs/EC_COMMAND_PROTOCOL_RE.md for full protocol details.
